units.title: Language Philosophy
units.tip: Zig is designed to be predictable and give you explicit control. Every operation is visible, no hidden behavior lurks in your code. This predictability makes systems programming safer and easier to reason about.

exercises.question: What does Zig mean by 'no hidden control flow'?
exercises.answer: No implicit function calls or exceptions; flow is only what you write
exercises.explain: Zig has no operator overloading, destructors or exceptions that silently call code you didn't write. Every flow decision comes from your code.
choices: No implicit function calls or exceptions; flow is only what you write
All code must use if-else only

exercises.question: How does Zig prevent hidden control flow?
exercises.answer: By removing operator overloading, exceptions, and hidden allocations
exercises.explain: Zig leaves out features like the operator overloading found in C++ that make it hard to see what code does. When you see a + b, it is plain arithmetic, not a hidden function call.
choices: By forcing you to write everything in assembly
By removing operator overloading, exceptions, and hidden allocations
By requiring all code to be single-threaded

exercises.question: What is the advantage of explicit allocation in Zig?
exercises.answer: You choose when and where memory happens, no garbage collector surprises
exercises.explain: With explicit allocation via allocators, there are no surprise garbage collection pauses or memory management decisions hidden from you. You are in control.
choices: It prevents all memory leaks automatically
You choose when and where memory happens, no garbage collector surprises

exercises.question: What is an allocator in Zig?
exercises.answer: An object passed to functions that defines how memory is allocated
exercises.explain: Allocators are passed explicitly to any function that needs memory. This makes it clear where allocation happens and lets you control the strategy.
choices: A built-in process that runs automatically
An object passed to functions that defines how memory is allocated

exercises.question: Why does Zig leave out operator overloading?
exercises.answer: So a + b is always plain arithmetic, never a hidden function call
exercises.explain: With overloading, a + b could run any code. Without it, an operator does only what it looks like, so you can read control flow straight from the source.
choices: So a + b is always plain arithmetic, never a hidden function call
Because overloading is impossible on computers

exercises.question: What resource does Zig handle explicitly?
exercises.answer: Memory, file handles, and other operating system resources
exercises.explain: Zig makes it your job to acquire and release resources. There is no implicit cleanup. This is safe when you use the right patterns.
choices: Memory, file handles, and other operating system resources
Nothing, Zig hides all resource management

exercises.question: How does Zig help you manage resources?
exercises.answer: Defer statements and manual cleanup patterns you write
exercises.explain: Zig provides defer to run cleanup code when a scope exits. You write the cleanup; Zig makes sure it runs.
choices: Defer statements and manual cleanup patterns you write

exercises.question: What is a defer statement in Zig?
exercises.answer: Code that runs when a scope exits, even on error
exercises.explain: Defer lets you write cleanup code right after resource acquisition. It runs when the scope exits, guaranteeing cleanup happens.
choices: Code that runs when a scope exits, even on error

exercises.question: Why is explicit resource management safer than implicit cleanup?
exercises.answer: You see exactly what happens and when, no surprises during cleanup
exercises.explain: When cleanup is explicit, you control when it happens and what order resources are freed. No hidden destructors run in unexpected order.
choices: You see exactly what happens and when, no surprises during cleanup

exercises.question: What design principle guides Zig's approach to resources?
exercises.answer: You own it, you manage it, nothing is hidden
exercises.explain: Zig's philosophy is that explicit control prevents bugs. You acquire resources, you decide when to release them.
choices: Resource management is impossible in systems languages
You own it, you manage it, nothing is hidden
Resources should be managed by the language automatically
Only the kernel can manage resources

units.title: Variables and Mutability
units.tip: Variables in Zig are either const (immutable) or var (mutable). Const means the value cannot change once assigned. This distinction catches bugs early and makes code intention clear.

exercises.question: What does const mean in Zig?
exercises.answer: The variable is immutable and cannot be reassigned
exercises.explain: A const variable is assigned once and cannot change. This prevents accidental modification and makes intent explicit.
choices: The variable is immutable and cannot be reassigned
The variable is mutable but hidden

exercises.question: What does var mean in Zig?
exercises.answer: The variable is mutable and can be reassigned
exercises.explain: A var variable can be assigned multiple times. Use var when you actually need to change the value.
choices: The variable is mutable and can be reassigned

exercises.question: When should you use const instead of var?
exercises.answer: When the value never changes after assignment
exercises.explain: Use const by default. Only use var when you actually reassign the variable. Const catches bugs and documents intent.
choices: When the value never changes after assignment

exercises.question: What does the type *const i32 mean?
exercises.answer: A pointer through which the i32 cannot be modified
exercises.explain: *const i32 is a pointer to an i32 that you can read but not write through. The pointer variable itself can still be reassigned if it is declared with var.
choices: A pointer through which the i32 cannot be modified
A pointer that can never be reassigned
A pointer that is always null
A pointer to a compile-time integer

exercises.question: What error does reassigning a const variable cause?
exercises.answer: A compile-time error
exercises.explain: The compiler catches const reassignments before your code runs. This prevents bugs early.
choices: No error, const is just documentation

exercises.question: What is variable shadowing?
exercises.answer: Declaring a new variable with the same name in an inner scope
exercises.explain: Shadowing is when an inner block reuses the name of an outer variable, hiding it in that scope. Zig does not allow it.
choices: Hiding a function from the compiler
Declaring a new variable with the same name in an inner scope

exercises.question: Is variable shadowing allowed in Zig?
exercises.answer: No, Zig reports a compile error when a name shadows another
exercises.explain: Many languages allow shadowing, but Zig rejects a local name that hides another one in an enclosing scope. This avoids confusing which variable you mean.
choices: Yes, Zig permits shadowing in nested scopes
No, Zig reports a compile error when a name shadows another

exercises.question: What is scope in Zig?
exercises.answer: The region of code where a variable is visible and accessible
exercises.explain: A variable is accessible from its declaration until the end of its scope. Scopes are delimited by blocks and functions.
choices: The region of code where a variable is visible and accessible
The amount of memory a variable uses

exercises.question: What happens when a variable goes out of scope?
exercises.answer: The variable is no longer accessible; defer blocks run
exercises.explain: When a scope ends, the variable is gone. Any defer statements in that scope run before the scope exits.
choices: The variable is deleted from memory
The variable is no longer accessible; defer blocks run
Nothing, the variable is still accessible

exercises.question: Can you access a variable outside its scope?
exercises.answer: No, the compiler prevents out-of-scope access
exercises.explain: Zig's compiler checks scope at compile time. Accessing a variable outside its scope is a compile error.
choices: Only if the variable is const
No, the compiler prevents out-of-scope access

units.title: Basic Types
units.tip: Zig has explicit types for integers (i32, u64), floats (f32, f64), booleans, and arrays. The type system is strict: mixing types usually needs an explicit cast. This prevents silent bugs.

exercises.question: What does i32 mean in Zig?
exercises.answer: A signed 32-bit integer
exercises.explain: i32 is a signed integer using 32 bits, ranging from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. The 'i' means signed, '32' is the bit width.

exercises.question: What does u64 mean in Zig?
exercises.answer: An unsigned 64-bit integer
exercises.explain: u64 is an unsigned integer using 64 bits, ranging from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. The 'u' means unsigned, '64' is the bit width.
choices: A pointer to an unsigned integer

exercises.question: What is the difference between i32 and u32?
exercises.answer: i32 is signed (negative allowed), u32 is unsigned (only positive)
exercises.explain: i32 can hold negative numbers but has a smaller positive range. u32 holds only non-negative numbers, so it can represent larger positive values.
choices: i32 is signed (negative allowed), u32 is unsigned (only positive)
Only if the type is known

exercises.question: What does f32 represent in Zig?
exercises.answer: A 32-bit floating-point number
exercises.explain: f32 is a single-precision float, similar to C's float. It uses 32 bits for approximate decimal numbers.

exercises.question: Can you implicitly convert i32 to f64 in Zig?
exercises.answer: No, you must use an explicit cast
exercises.explain: Zig does not coerce types automatically. Converting an integer to a float requires an explicit cast like @floatFromInt().
choices: No, you must use an explicit cast

exercises.question: What is an array in Zig?
exercises.answer: A fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type
exercises.explain: An array has a length known at compile time, and all elements share one type. It lives wherever its variable lives, such as on the stack or inside a struct.
choices: A fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type

exercises.question: What is the type of an array with 10 integers?
exercises.explain: [10]i32 means an array of exactly 10 signed 32-bit integers. The size is part of the type.

exercises.question: What is a pointer in Zig?
exercises.answer: A variable holding the memory address of another value
exercises.explain: A pointer stores an address. You dereference it with .* to access the value it points to. Pointers are explicit.
choices: A reference that is always safe
A variable holding the memory address of another value

exercises.question: What is the type of a pointer to i32?
exercises.explain: *i32 is a pointer to a signed 32-bit integer. The * prefix denotes a pointer type.

exercises.question: What is a slice in Zig?
exercises.answer: A view into a contiguous part of an array or buffer
exercises.explain: A slice is a pointer plus a length. It lets you work with part of an array without knowing the full size at compile time.
choices: A type that cannot be used
A view into a contiguous part of an array or buffer

units.title: Functions
units.tip: Functions in Zig are declared with explicit parameter and return types. They are composable building blocks. Zig supports recursion, optional return values, and error returns.

exercises.question: How do you declare a function in Zig?
exercises.answer: fn name(params) type { body }
exercises.explain: Zig functions start with fn, followed by a name, parameters, return type, and a block. Parameters and return type are required.

exercises.question: What does a function parameter declaration look like?
exercises.answer: name: type
exercises.explain: Each parameter is declared with a name, a colon, and its type, like x: i32. Multiple parameters are separated by commas.

exercises.question: Can you have a function with no parameters?
exercises.answer: Yes, you must still specify the return type
exercises.explain: Functions with no parameters still need a return type. The parameter list is empty: fn foo() i32 { return 42; }
choices: Yes, you must still specify the return type
No, functions need at least one parameter
Only if the function has no body

exercises.question: What is the difference between parameters and arguments?
exercises.answer: Parameters are declared in the function; arguments are passed when calling
exercises.explain: fn add(a: i32, b: i32) has parameters. When you call add(3, 5), 3 and 5 are arguments.
choices: Arguments are types, parameters are values
Parameters are declared in the function; arguments are passed when calling

exercises.question: Are function parameters mutable in Zig?
exercises.answer: No, they are const by default and cannot be reassigned
exercises.explain: Function parameters are const. If you need to modify a parameter, you assign it to a new var variable.
choices: No, they are const by default and cannot be reassigned

exercises.question: How do you return a value from a function in Zig?
exercises.answer: Use a return statement with the value
exercises.explain: return value; sends the value back to the caller. The type must match the declared return type.
choices: Use a return statement with the value

exercises.question: Can a function return multiple values in Zig?
exercises.answer: Yes, by returning a struct with multiple fields
exercises.explain: A Zig function returns a single value. To return several, return a struct holding them.
choices: Yes, by returning a struct with multiple fields
Yes, with a comma-separated return list

exercises.question: What is recursion?
exercises.answer: A function calling itself to solve a problem
exercises.explain: Recursion breaks a problem into smaller versions of itself. Each recursive call should move closer to a base case that stops the recursion.
choices: A function calling itself to solve a problem

exercises.question: What is a base case in recursion?
exercises.answer: The condition that stops recursive calls and returns directly
exercises.explain: The base case is the simplest version of the problem that doesn't require recursion. Without it, recursion never stops.
choices: The condition that stops recursive calls and returns directly

exercises.question: Can Zig functions be recursive?
exercises.answer: Yes, a function can call itself, but very deep recursion can overflow the stack
exercises.explain: Zig allows recursion. Each call uses stack space, so recursion needs a base case and a reasonable depth.
choices: Yes, a function can call itself, but very deep recursion can overflow the stack

units.title: Error Handling
units.tip: Zig uses error unions, with try and catch, for error handling. An error union can hold either a value or an error. The try keyword propagates errors up the call stack. This makes errors visible and explicit.

exercises.question: What is an error union in Zig?
exercises.answer: A type that can hold either a value or an error
exercises.explain: An error union combines a value type and an error set. It represents an operation that might fail.
choices: A type that can hold either a value or an error

exercises.question: What is the syntax for an error union type?
exercises.answer: !ValueType or ErrorSet!ValueType
exercises.explain: ! joins an error set and a value type. For example, !i32 is an i32 that can fail, and FileOpenError!File names exactly which errors can occur.

exercises.question: How must you handle an error union before using its value?
exercises.answer: Unwrap it with try or catch, or use if with an else |err| branch
exercises.explain: Use try to propagate the error, catch to handle it, or if/else to branch on it. Using an error union as a plain value is a compile error.
choices: Unwrap it with try or catch, or use if with an else |err| branch

exercises.question: What does try do when given an error union?
exercises.answer: Returns the value if success, propagates the error if failure
exercises.explain: try unwraps the value on success, or immediately returns the error to the caller on failure.
choices: Returns the value if success, propagates the error if failure

exercises.question: Can a function return an error union?
exercises.answer: Yes, it declares the return type as an error union
exercises.explain: A function can return ErrorSet!ValueType. Callers must handle the error or propagate it with try.
choices: Yes, it declares the return type as an error union

exercises.question: What does the try keyword do?
exercises.answer: Unwraps an error union; returns from the function on error
exercises.explain: try extracts the value from an error union. If an error occurs, try stops execution and returns the error to the caller.
choices: Unwraps an error union; returns from the function on error

exercises.question: How do you use catch in Zig?
exercises.answer: expression catch |err| handler
exercises.explain: catch runs if the expression is an error. The err variable holds the error, and handler is code that runs on error.

exercises.question: What does catch do when the expression succeeds?
exercises.answer: Nothing, it passes the value through and does not run
exercises.explain: catch only runs when an error occurs. If the expression succeeds, catch is skipped.
choices: It converts the value to an error
Nothing, it passes the value through and does not run

exercises.question: Can you ignore an error with catch?
exercises.answer: Yes, catch can supply a default value instead
exercises.explain: foo() catch 0 uses 0 whenever foo() fails. Substituting a value like this is a form of handling, but do it deliberately, not carelessly.
choices: Yes, catch can supply a default value instead
No, you must handle all errors

exercises.question: What is the difference between try and catch?
exercises.answer: Try propagates the error; catch handles it locally
exercises.explain: try stops and returns the error to the caller. catch runs your code to handle the error without propagating it.
choices: Try propagates the error; catch handles it locally

units.title: Advanced Concepts
units.tip: Optionals represent values that might not exist. Comptime runs code at compile time for meta-programming. Manual memory management via allocators gives you precise control. C interop lets you call C libraries directly.

exercises.question: What is an optional in Zig?
exercises.answer: A value that might be null or hold a real value
exercises.explain: An optional type like ?i32 can hold either an i32 or null. It is safer than C's null pointers because the type system tracks nullability.
choices: A value that might be null or hold a real value

exercises.question: What is the syntax for an optional type?
exercises.answer: ?ValueType
exercises.explain: ? means the value can be null or a ValueType. For example, ?i32 is either null or an i32.

exercises.question: What does comptime mean in Zig?
exercises.answer: Code that runs at compile time to generate or compute results
exercises.explain: comptime evaluates expressions during compilation, not at runtime. This enables meta-programming and compile-time computation.
choices: Code that runs at compile time to generate or compute results

exercises.question: Why would you use comptime?
exercises.answer: To compute values once at compile time instead of every run
exercises.explain: comptime reduces runtime work by doing calculations, unrolling loops, or generating code once when the program is built.
choices: To compute values once at compile time instead of every run

exercises.question: Can an optional value hold an error?
exercises.answer: No, optionals hold null or a value; errors use error unions
exercises.explain: Optionals represent presence or absence. Error unions represent success or failure with a specific error.
choices: No, optionals hold null or a value; errors use error unions
Yes, optionals and errors are the same

exercises.question: How do you allocate memory in Zig?
exercises.answer: Ask an allocator you pass in, using calls like alloc or create
exercises.explain: Allocators are passed to functions that need memory. This makes allocation visible and lets you control where memory comes from.
choices: Ask an allocator you pass in, using calls like alloc or create

exercises.question: Who frees memory you allocate with an allocator in Zig?
exercises.answer: You do, explicitly, often with defer
exercises.explain: Zig has no garbage collector. You release memory yourself, usually by writing defer allocator.free(...) right after allocating.
choices: You do, explicitly, often with defer
The compiler, at the end of the scope

exercises.question: What is stack allocation in Zig?
exercises.answer: Memory allocated on the stack; freed automatically when scope exits
exercises.explain: Stack variables are allocated on the stack and freed when the function returns. No manual deallocation needed.
choices: Memory allocated on the stack; freed automatically when scope exits

exercises.question: Can Zig call C functions?
exercises.answer: Yes, by declaring extern functions or importing C headers
exercises.explain: Zig can call C libraries by declaring extern function signatures or importing C headers. C types can be used directly.
choices: Yes, by declaring extern functions or importing C headers

exercises.question: Why would you use C interop in Zig?
exercises.answer: To use existing C libraries and existing mature code
exercises.explain: C libraries are mature and battle-tested. Zig can leverage them without reimplementing functionality.
choices: To use existing C libraries and existing mature code
